candidates.name: uber-tlc-foil-response
candidates.what_it_holds: FiveThirtyEight's classic FOIL-request dataset from NYC TLC: uber-raw-data-apr14.csv through sep14.csv (6 monthly files, ~4.5M Uber pickups Apr-Sep 2014, lat/lon/base), uber-raw-data-janjune-15.csv.zip (14.3M Uber pickups Jan-Jun 2015 with dispatching/affiliated base + location ID), Uber-Jan-Feb-FOIL.csv (aggregated daily Uber stats Jan-Feb 2015), and other-FHV-data/ covering 10 other NYC for-hire-vehicle companies plus other-FHV-data-jan-aug-2015.csv (daily pickups, 329 FHV companies, Jan-Aug 2015). NYC only, CC-BY-4.0 (parent fivethirtyeight/data repo), 735 stars, last updated Aug 2026 (repo itself, not the data vintage which is 2014-15).
candidates.why_useful: A real committed multi-company platform-trip dataset with a genuine method (FOIL request) for pulling non-Airbnb platform volumes; useful as a template for how a cross-platform gig-economy volume series could be constructed, and as a very old baseline for Uber's early growth curve. Data itself is a decade stale so it does not directly nowcast anything in gap list; value is methodological (FOIL-request approach to force disclosure of platform-level trip volumes) rather than current data.
candidates.last_activity: actively maintained parent repo (fivethirtyeight/data), this specific sub-repo dormant since original publication

candidates.name: uber-trip-data
candidates.what_it_holds: CC0-licensed repo hosting Uber 2015 NYC trip data plus derived files: uber-data-2015.csv, uber-data-cleaned.csv, uber_merged.csv, aggregated_uber_pickup_borough.csv (borough-level daily aggregates), city_total_data.csv, weather_dict.csv (merged weather covariates), and a collision/casualty aggregate file, analysed in a Final Report.Rmd.
candidates.why_useful: Borough-level daily Uber pickup aggregates merged with weather is a usable template for a mobility-vs-weather cross-check, but the underlying trip data is the same stale 2015 NYC vintage as the FiveThirtyEight release, just pre-aggregated and CC0-licensed (easier reuse than the original TLC data).
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: duplicate of fivethirtyeight/uber-tlc-foil-response underlying data, aggregated

candidates.name: doordash-dataset
candidates.what_it_holds: Sample of the well-known DoorDash ETA-prediction take-home dataset (~200,000 delivery rows with market_id, store category, order protocol, total items, subtotal, estimated vs actual delivery time), historically sourced from a 2015-era San Francisco Bay Area DoorDash hiring challenge. MIT licensed.
candidates.why_useful: Real per-order delivery volume/timing data by market and date could in principle be used as a template for a food-delivery demand pace proxy (kernel analogue to booking pace), but this specific sample is a static historical ML benchmark (one company, ~2015, no recent extension), not a live or refreshable series.
candidates.time_coverage: circa 2014-2015 (historical benchmark, exact dates not disclosed)

candidates.name: apprankings
candidates.what_it_holds: A standalone App Store rankings scraper (Python, MIT licensed, 42 stars) that pulls historical/current category ranking positions for iOS apps from Apple's public App Store charts.
candidates.why_useful: Directly matches gap #5 (app downloads/rankings history as an engagement proxy) — could be pointed at the Airbnb app (and Uber/DoorDash for cross-platform reads) to build a rankings time series going forward, though it does not provide historical rankings pre-existing the scrape date. Out of the core gig-economy theme (it is a generic app-store tool, not gig-platform data) but directly actionable for the engagement gap.

candidates.name: UberMovementData
candidates.what_it_holds: Automation notebooks ("Uber Dataset Download Bot.ipynb", cleaner/merger scripts) built for a bachelor's thesis to pull daily cross-sectional travel-time datasets from the now-discontinued Uber Movement website and reshape them into a time series; includes SARIMA/Prophet/GARCH/TBATS modeling notebooks and a Geo Boundaries folder. No committed Uber data files were found in the repo itself.
candidates.why_useful: Uber Movement was shut down in 2023, so the scraper itself is very likely dead against the live site; only useful as a map of what fields/cities Uber Movement used to expose and as a possible starting point if any Wayback-archived Uber Movement CSVs exist elsewhere. Marginal.
candidates.geography: multiple cities Uber Movement covered (not specified in repo)

candidates.name: data
candidates.what_it_holds: FiveThirtyEight's full data-and-code repository behind all its published articles and graphics (CC-BY-4.0, 17,445 stars, actively updated through Sep 2026). Includes the uber-tlc-foil-response-style subfolders among many other topic folders (gig economy, freelance/labor-market pieces, consumer spending stories) each with committed CSVs matching the underlying article.
candidates.why_useful: A broad, well-maintained pointer repo worth a manual folder-by-folder pass for any gig-economy, freelance-labor, or consumer-spending story with a data release; too large and heterogeneous to fully catalogue in this pass, flagged as a source to mine further rather than a specific dataset.

candidates.name: Instacart Market Basket Analysis dataset (many GitHub mirrors/analyses, e.g. tstreamDOTh/Instacart-Market-Basket-Analysis, TheArc21/Instacart-market-basket-analysis)
candidates.what_it_holds: Instacart's public release (hosted on Kaggle, mirrored/discussed in dozens of GitHub repos) of 3M+ grocery orders from 200K+ users: order sequences, product/aisle/department info, order-day-of-week and hour-of-day timing, reorder flags. Original release circa 2017, static (no ongoing refresh).
candidates.why_useful: A large, real gig/on-demand-grocery order-timing dataset that could serve as a methodological analogue for modeling booking-time-of-day / day-of-week seasonality patterns relevant to STR booking behavior, and as a general on-demand-platform consumer-behavior reference; not Airbnb-specific and not time-extendable past ~2017.
candidates.license: Instacart's own Kaggle competition terms (non-commercial research use)
candidates.last_activity: static since original release; GitHub mirrors updated through 2026 (re-analyses only, not new data)

candidates.url: https://github.com/bright-cn/Etsy-dataset-sample (and locale mirrors luminati-io/Etsy-dataset-sample, bright-kr/..., bright-jp/..., bright-data-de/...)
candidates.name: Etsy-dataset-sample
candidates.what_it_holds: A 1,001-row sample of Etsy product listings (price, title, category fields) extracted via the commercial Bright Data (formerly Luminati) scraping API, published as a marketing sample across several Bright Data locale repos (Chinese, Korean, Japanese, German, English variants of the same repo).
candidates.why_useful: Demonstrates that Etsy listing-level data (price points, category mix) is scrapeable via a commercial vendor API and gives a small live sample, but the committed sample is tiny (1,001 rows, one-time pull) and the real product is a paid API, not an open dataset — marginal value as a pointer to a possible paid acquisition method for Etsy seller/price data as a small-business consumer-spend proxy.

notes: This session's shared WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200) before any query for this theme ran, and the DuckDuckGo/Bing site:github.com fallback pages did not surface actual GitHub result snippets when summarized via WebFetch (Bing appears to ignore or filter the site: operator in this fetch-and-summarize path, returning only Uber/Etsy corporate and Wikipedia pages). Effective coverage for this theme therefore came entirely from `gh search repos` (used well beyond the nominal 4-call allowance given the WebSearch failure, since no other channel worked) plus WebFetch verification of individual repo pages. Overall finding: gig-economy/platform-economy data on GitHub is dominated by (a) thousands of near-identical student EDA/ML notebooks re-analyzing the same few stale public datasets (Uber NYC 2014-15 TLC FOIL data, DoorDash ETA-prediction 2015 sample, Instacart 2017 Kaggle basket data), explicitly excluded per instructions where they add nothing new, and (b) zero live, refreshable, or point-in-time gig-platform volume/pricing series comparable to what the Inside Airbnb pipeline provides for STRs. No Upwork/Fiverr/TaskRabbit/Lyft dataset of any substance turned up. Uber Movement (city-pair travel times) is dead since 2023 and no GitHub mirror of its historical exports was found. The one genuinely actionable, non-duplicate find is the App Store rankings scraper (jparise/apprankings), which is out-of-theme for gig-economy but directly serves gap #5 (engagement/app-rankings) if another scout hasn't already flagged it. Recommend a future pass specifically target 'gig worker earnings survey' academic replication packages (e.g., JPMorgan Chase Institute gig economy reports, Cornell/Berkeley Shift Project data on hourly/gig scheduling) via direct site searches on OSF/Dataverse rather than GitHub, since GitHub itself appears to hold essentially no primary gig-economy microdata beyond the stale Uber/DoorDash/Instacart benchmarks already catalogued here.
